titleStmt.title: Exploring U.S. Latina Women's Literature: Cataloging Latinidad in a Digital Collection

dhq:bio.p: Monika Dabrowska holds a PhD in Hispanic Literature and is an Associate Professor at the Universidad Internacional de La Rioja (UNIR). Her research focuses on Latin American literatures, U.S. Latina/o literature and culture, ecopoetics, women’s writing, artificial intelligence, and the digital humanities. Her work has been published in leading journals, including Digital Scholarship in the Humanities, Reviews in Digital Humanities, RILCE, Bulletin of Hispanic Studies and Studia Neophilologica, among others.

dhq:abstract.p: This article critically examines the development of a digital corpus dedicated to the literary production of Latina/Chicana authors in the United States, published by Arte Público Press (APP) over the past four decades (1980–2024). The project US Latina Writers Published by Arte Público Press, created using CollectionBuilder, gathers metadata about fiction and nonfiction texts across multiple genres, including narrative, poetry, drama, essays, interviews, and illustrated works. It aims to map the literary contributions of US Latina/Chicana writers, whose extensive and diverse body of work remains largely underrecognized by both the general public and literary scholarship in the United States and Europe. This presentation offers a theoretical and methodological reflection on the potential and limitations of a digital exhibition built with CollectionBuilder. It focuses particularly on the practical challenges of data stewardship, especially concerning gender, race, class, and ethnicity, within the framework of digital ethnic and feminist studies. The project serves as a concrete example of how marginalized perspectives and voices can be integrated into the digital sphere, advancing equity and justice in the representation of Latina/Chicana literatures. The article also offers a critical analysis of the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) assigned to these works, demonstrating how this controlled vocabulary structurally underrepresents the plural, intersectional, and evolving dimensions of Latina identity. In doing so, it contributes to ongoing debates in digital humanities, feminist data studies, and U.S. Latina/o literary scholarship by illustrating how metadata practices shape the visibility, classification, and interpretation of marginalized literary traditions.

dhq:teaser.p: How do digital collections shape the visibility of U.S. Latina and Chicana women's literature? This article explores a digital collection of works published by Arte Público Press, examining how metadata, classification systems, and feminist data practices can challenge the underrepresentation of Latina writers and open new pathways for literary discovery.

div.head: TESTING 1. Introduction
div.p: This article presents a project dedicated to the creation of a digital collection, US Latina Writers, The project has been commented on by Kelly Kreitz in Reviews in Digital Humanities. that compiles the literary works of Latin American women authors in the United States, published by Arte Público Press over the past four decades (1980–2024). Or, more precisely, an interactive interface built upon a metadata collection representing a defined subset of the Arte Público catalog . Affiliated with the University of Houston, Arte Público Press is a pioneering publisher of Latinx literature in the U.S. and has served as a crucial forum for the dissemination of Hispanic culture in North America. Beyond its editorial contributions, the press has played a fundamental role in identifying, documenting, and preserving the literary heritage of Latinx authors throughout U.S. literary history, spanning from colonial literature to contemporary works, with particular emphasis on the 19th century and the Chicano civil rights movements of the 1960s and 1970s. These efforts were further institutionalized in 1992 with the establishment of the Recovering the U.S. Hispanic Literary Heritage program, alongside the publication of numerous anthologies, critical editions, conference proceedings, and digital initiatives.

Among the press's landmark publications is The House on Mango Street, Sandra Cisneros's novel, regarded as one of the foundational texts of contemporary Chicana literature. The press has also published widely recognized authors such as Tato Laviera, Rolando Hinojosa, Tomás Rivera, Víctor Villaseñor, Miguel Piñero, and Mario Bencastro. Additionally, it has been a pivotal platform for the work of renowned women writers, including Ana Castillo, Lorna Dee Cervantes, Judith Ortiz Cofer, Nicholasa Mohr, Helena María Viramontes, and Lucha Corpi, among many others. The literary works of authors categorized as U.S. Latin Americans, despite their vast and diverse output, remain an underexplored field in U.S. literary studies and merit greater attention from both readers and the academic community. In this context, the initiative to compile a digital exhibit of all the books authored by women and published by Arte Público Press emerges, with the aim of disseminating and promoting this literary production.

The digital collection focuses on women’s literature and encompasses both fiction and nonfiction texts across various genres, including narrative, poetry, drama, and anthologies. In total, it brings together 130 literary works and 11 anthologies by over 75 Chicana and Latina authors. Among the included texts are historical works by authors from the 19th and early 20th centuries — such as María Amparo Ruiz de Burton (1832–1895), Leonor Villegas de Magnón (1876–1955), Luisa Capetillo (1879–1922), and María Cristina Mena (1893–1965) — as well as works by contemporary authors. It is important to note that many of these writers remained unknown or were overlooked until their legacies were rescued through the Recovering the U.S. Hispanic Literary Heritage project and edited within the specific series of the same name. The project provides information about the literary works of Latina authors, who primarily write in English, though also in Spanish, and includes works translated between both languages, as well as bilingual editions. Its purpose extends beyond merely disseminating and popularizing this literary heritage in digital format; it aims to generate documented knowledge about Hispanic literature in the U.S. and foster new interpretative approaches through digital tools and methods.

This article has a twofold objective. First, it outlines the process of constructing the digital archive using CollectionBuilder and situates this work within the broader framework of Latina Digital Humanities. It presents the results achieved as well as an assessment of the possibilities and limitations of the tool employed. Second, it offers a critical reflection on the challenges involved in disseminating the literary legacy of the authors included in the project and in facilitating research on their works and thematic concerns. Finally, the study considers the project’s future directions and its potential impact on the study and dissemination of the literary legacy of Latina authors in the United States.

div.head: 2. Contextualizing US Latina Women Writers in U.S. Latino Digital Humanities
div.p: Before proceeding, it is worth clarifying the difference between Latin American literature and U.S. Latina/o literature. The latter designates the national literatures of Latin American countries. The former constitutes a distinct field, produced within the United States, largely though not exclusively in English or bilingual and code-switching registers, and shaped by histories of immigration, territorial annexation and colonization, civil rights movements, and racialization specific to Latina/o communities in this country . The authors gathered here, though of Latin American heritage, are U.S.-based and predominantly English-dominant or bilingual, writing from within and in critical dialogue with U.S. literary and political contexts. For this reason, we situate them within the established field of U.S. Latina/o literature rather than treating them as expatriate or diasporic voices within Latin American letters . Latin American women authors in the U.S. constitute a fundamental part of the country’s literary heritage and possess great creative potential; however, their visibility remains limited. As Güereña noted years ago, there is a marked lack of representation in the Chicano literary tradition, prompting questions about the reasons behind this situation. In his analysis, he responded:

p.quote: Mainstream literary historians therefore had a long history of ignoring Chicano writings, perhaps due to a perceived linguistic obstacle, however Cecil Robinson attributes this lack of interest to a socio-political polarization of the White and Chicano society which resulted from a rejection of the Chicano in and by this country .

div.p: Furthermore, the author added the limited interest of libraries, which generally neglected to collect and preserve the materials being generated by the Chicano community . While his study primarily focused on Chicano archives and manuscripts, it can be asserted that the printed book suffers the same fate — particularly when written in Spanish. Contemporary Spanish literature lives on the margins and is not readily circulated in the United States, observe . They further add: The absence of Latinx Spanish literary texts directly affects the academic discourse around what is Latinx literature of the United States .

The cultural production of this group, historically considered a minority or ethnic group, continues to face numerous sociopolitical, linguistic, economic, and academic challenges, in addition to the deep-rooted prejudices and stereotypes embedded in society and the publishing industry. However, in the 21st century, these voices, which for so long remained silenced, have begun to resonate more powerfully and clearly, due to the confluence of various factors . So much so, that the term New Latino Boom, coined by , can be used to describe the growing impact of Latinx literature in the United States. Today, readers can engage with the original and socially committed works of several generations of talented women authors, sometimes overshadowed by Latino writers who have received prestigious awards such as the Pulitzer Prize — although these remain few — and other literary recognitions.

In this context, Chicana and Latina women authors have enriched the literary expression of womanhood and the subjectivity of Latinas in the United States. The writers featured in this collection, such as Ana Castillo, Alicia Gaspar de Alba, Emma Pérez, and many others, have played a pivotal role in the decolonization of this identity and in the construction of U.S. Latina/Chicano feminist thought. Regarding this female contribution, Avilés emphasizes that women have generated methodologies that contribute to a robust understanding of the benefits of embracing intermixed, intersectional, and complex states of communication . Other writers explore themes related to regional and cultural differences, inherited and transformed traditions, family and generational relationships, social barriers, women’s struggles, and networks of female support, among many others. These concerns stem from a long tradition of self-determination, resistance, and survival within Latina/o or Hispanic communities in the United States.

Despite having produced a vast and multifaceted corpus, these authors remain underrepresented in cultural historiography and literary studies, both within the United States and abroad. This project seeks to address this ongoing lack of public visibility by providing information and digital access to forgotten or lesser-known texts, both historical and contemporary. In doing so, it contributes to bridging the gap in the recognition of Latina writers in the U.S., bringing their legacy to the forefront and highlighting their contributions to the literary and cultural fields. Additionally, the project aligns with a broader effort to decolonize "American" national narratives and, consequently, contribute to the decolonization of digital humanities .

The intersection of Latinx literary studies in the United States and Digital Humanities is a key aspect of this project. The representation of this marginalized community within a Digital Humanities initiative connects with various theoretical approaches, such as Latina Feminism, Latinx Digital Humanities (; ; ), Data Feminism (), and Intersectional DH Feminism (). First and foremost, the representation of the literary history of Latina women in a digital environment, through an open-access database, significantly expands the possibilities for dissemination and research of the gathered corpus. In this regard, the project can be seen as an act of decentralizing dominant narratives within the field of Digital Humanities and shifting U.S. Latin American Literature — and specifically that created by women — from margin to center. As D’Ignazio and Klein put it, the voices of those who speak from the margins, whether because of their gender, sexuality, race, ability, class, geographic location, or any combination of those (and other) subject positions .

Given the nature of the content compiled in the collection, it is essential to represent and analyze it from an intersectional perspective that considers the interplay of factors such as language, race, gender, and citizenship within the digital space. In this regard, the project is framed within an intersectional feminist approach in the field of Digital Humanities. As D’Ignazio and Klein remind us, Indeed, feminism must be intersectional if it seeks to address the challenges of the present moment . The work developed in this project aligns with this feminist and intersectional approach within Digital Humanities, adopting its methods and practices to create a more open and inclusive initiative.

As far as we know, there are still relatively few specifically literary digital projects in the field of Latinx Digital Humanities. While numerous important initiatives have been created dedicated to activism and civil rights (e.g., Chicana/o Activism in the Southern Plains Through Time and Space), the border experience (The Border Studies Archive, Mapping Violence), history and art (Latino Murals in the U.S., Picturing Mexican America), or even periodicals (Latin American Anarchist and Labour Periodicals Online, Borderlands Archives Cartography) — to name just a few, as it is impossible to provide a comprehensive overview here — few have focused on literary works. Even fewer center on the literary production of U.S. Latinas.
Among the few initiatives similar to our project is the Hispanic Theater Collection/ Colección de teatro hispano (cf. ), dedicated to theatrical works, and A Visual History of Chicano/a/x Literatures by Martín-Rodríguez, which primarily focuses on bibliographic compilation and visual representation of book covers rather than exploration of literary content. The literary compilation that most closely resembles our project is Mapa de escritoras mexicanas contemporáneas (), as it also includes authors residing in and writing from the United States. Finally, Hablemos Escritoras, directed by Adriana Pacheco, provides an important example for the digital dissemination of Latin American and Latina women’s literary works. Likewise GeoTestimonios Transfronterizos, developed by Sylvia Fernández and Gris Muñoz, showcases transborder literary works by women writers from border regions.

div.head: 3. Why CollectionBuilder for U.S. Latina Writers?
div.p: After outlining the context of Latina women’s literature and reviewing comparable initiatives in the field of Digital Humanities, it became necessary to select an appropriate tool for making a digital collection accessible to a broad and interested audience, including readers, researchers, and educators. The aim is to provide users with diverse forms of information and digital objects, as well as opportunities for cultural, philological, and pedagogical exploration. This project requires an open-access platform that treats metadata as primary content, enhances the discoverability of images and texts, and enables the creation of engaging, browsable visualizations — such as timelines, maps, facets, and item pages — for both scholars and the general public

The decision to adopt CollectionBuilder, rather than general-purpose platforms (such as WordPress, Joomla, or Drupal) or more specialized systems (such as Scalar or Mukurtu), arises from the specific requirements of this project: a bibliographic corpus, a robust metadata layer, transparent data workflows, and a low-cost sustainability plan. The U.S. Latina Writers project is not a traditional institutional repository, a web portal, or an exhibit builder designed for large audiovisual collections. Instead, we prioritize minimal computing solutions that do not rely on expensive infrastructures and that provide out-of-the-box tools and open up new possibilities for representation of material from minoritized communities in the digital cultural record . In this context, we value ease of access, data transparency (via open CSV/JSON files), and long-term sustainability that does not require a dedicated server. These needs diverge significantly from those addressed by general CMS platforms, such as Drupal, WordPress, or Joomla, which are built for page-oriented content rather than metadata-driven collections and often lack data transparency while imposing ongoing server and maintenance costs. Scalar, for its part, performs poorly with tabular data and is better suited for multimedia commentaries and pedagogical narratives. Mukurtu is specifically designed to host culturally sensitive materials and community-managed archives; as such, it is not an appropriate platform for an open-access literary bibliography.

On the other hand, we also evaluated static-site generators (SSGs) such as Eleventy (), Hugo,
For a case study on the creation of the Recetas de las Américas website using the Hugo static-site generator, see .
Gatsby, and Wax, all of which share a minimal-computing philosophy.
However, these tools often require more complex deployment strategies, for example, the Jekyll–IIIF configuration used in Wax. Within this group, CollectionBuilder stands out as a low–technical-barrier option. For library digital repositories and exhibits, Omeka is a widely used platform, but its server and database dependencies: PHP, MySQL, hosted server environments, and regular updates often require institution-level support. DSpace is well suited for large-scale institutional repositories, but this project does not fall within that scope. Greenstone, which relies on Java-based interfaces, offers less contemporary web design and limited mobile responsiveness. Fundamentally, Omeka, DSpace, and Greenstone exceed the infrastructural needs of this project.

CollectionBuilder brings together the key strengths of open-source platforms: minimal computing principles, economic sustainability, data transparency, and scholarly openness, while avoiding the limitations commonly associated with general-purpose CMSs and repository platforms. To justify this choice, it is useful to situate CollectionBuilder within the comparative CMS landscape outlined by , who evaluates platforms such as WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, DSpace, Omeka, and Greenstone across a range of criteria, including cost, usability, community support, customizability, documentation quality, multilingual capacity, security, scalability, and interoperability. While Kar’s study never mentions CollectionBuilder, an omission that itself points to the emergence of minimal computing ecosystems beyond traditional library CMS.

Developed by the University of Idaho, CollectionBuilder was designed specifically to create websites that host digital collections and exhibitions. It adheres to the principles of GLAM institutions (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums), which promote open access to digitized materials. The tool is open source, built with the Jekyll static-site generator, and grounded in a static-web, minimal-computing approach. According to , this philosophy encourages the use of open tools and open data, ensuring that metadata remain reusable and shareable while giving creators full control over their data and content. This orientation aligns closely with the values of our project, which seeks to disseminate Latina literature in an open and inclusive manner.

Another reason for choosing CollectionBuilder was the attractive design of its interface, which allows for the combination of texts with graphic elements (images in JPEG and PNG formats) and audio elements (MP3 files). Regarding the visualization of information, the tool offers four main types of representations: a) topic clouds (displaying Subject and Location tags), b) maps based on geolocation coordinates, c) timelines based on the dates of the objects, and d) data tables, with the option to filter metadata or download it in Excel or CSV formats. The main page of the portal takes the form of an infographic-style summary of the gathering’s contents, providing users with a clear and dynamic view of the material. Additionally, CollectionBuilder can integrate with CONTENTdm to produce a public-facing interface and customized metadata visualizations that support exploratory research .

div.head: 4. Data preparation and curation
div.p: The project was developed in two phases: the first focused on data extraction and completion of the metadata form in CSV format, and the second dedicated to the development of the collection’s interface on GitHub. Several preliminary tasks were carried out for the implementation of the project.

First, it was necessary to select the works to be included in the collection. The decision was made to include all books authored by women published by Arte Público Press since its inception, with the exception of children’s and young adult titles published in the Piñata Books series since its creation in 1994. This exclusion was based on two main reasons: first, the decision to focus the project on an adult audience; and second, because work has already begun on a specific exhibition for this group of texts within CollectionBuilder. It was determined that the exhibition would include titles published in both English and Spanish, as well as those translated or published in bilingual editions, encompassing all literary genres: poetry, drama, and narrative, including fiction and non-fiction books (autobiography, biography, essay). To carry out the selection, the Arte Público Press database was explored, and, to cross-check the results, the Library of Congress (LC) catalog was also consulted, applying filters by publisher. After this process of refinement, a total of 141 works by 75 different authors, spanning various genres, were selected.

A second initial task involved determining the fields that should be included in the data sheet to adequately represent the information on the website we were going to create. Considering the features of CollectionBuilder and the types of visualizations this tool allows, the goal was to decide what additional information would be useful for users when exploring the collection. This determined the metadata that needed to be collected, including biobibliographical information, as well as details related to the categorization of works by genre and keywords, summaries, or information about translations. In creating the metadata sheet, we of course took into account the standard CollectionBuilder template, which requires four mandatory fields: objectid, filename, title, and format. In addition to these columns, it was deemed necessary to include further information such as the publication date of each work, the translator (if applicable), the literary genre, a brief summary, topics, and descriptive tags. Furthermore, the option to create maps required the inclusion of data regarding the locations where the plot of the literary works unfolds.

With all this data, a spreadsheet was created in Excel (file “metadata-template.csv”) to systematize all the relevant information. Finally, the following fields were included: identifier, filename, title, creator, translator, genre, description, publication date, location, latitude, longitude, subject, tags, language, format, rights, and rights statement. The columns for title, description, location, subject, and tags were expanded in both English and Spanish, in anticipation of a bilingual edition version of the website’s interface.

figure.head: Screenshot of the Excel metadata-template with the above-mentioned fields and information.
figure.figDesc: The spreadsheet organizes the bibliographic and descriptive fields used to document literary works and support their search, classification, and visualization within the collection.

div.p: From that point, the process of cleaning and curating the data began. Although it might have appeared to be a mechanical task, we soon realized that creating this database required making several crucial decisions that would affect the final outcome. One of the initial challenges arose in standardizing the author data (the "creator" column). The names of the authors were not always presented uniformly: sometimes they included a middle name or initial, while at other times, such elements were omitted. Initially, we aimed to be exhaustive in gathering the most complete information possible. Ultimately, however, we chose to adhere to the version provided by the author to the publisher at the time of publication. For example, we recorded "Alba Ambert" rather than "Alba Nydia Ambert," and "Denise Chávez" rather than "Denise Elia Chávez." We also maintained the use — or omission — of a second surname, especially when it pertained to a spouse’s surname, as in the case of "Jovita González" instead of "Jovita González Mireles."

A similar dilemma arose regarding the authors’ dates of birth. Initially, we considered that including this data might be useful for creating a timeline to order the writers by generation, given that at least three distinct age groups can already be identified. However, in some cases, this information proved difficult to obtain because it was not publicly available, as was the case with Yolanda Gallardo, Teresa Bevin, Tina Juárez, and others. At one point, we contemplated including the birthdate only when it was available on the author’s Library of Congress record. Nevertheless, noticing that these gaps would preclude a comprehensive chronological representation, we ultimately decided to forgo this option.

On the other hand, we considered it important to extract information regarding the birthplace or country of origin of the authors, with the aim of enabling the filtering of works based on the authors' ancestry. While in some cases this label could be easily incorporated — since such information was readily available on the book’s back cover or through digital sources like Wikipedia — in other instances, completing this field proved challenging. For example, it was straightforward to label Lucha Corpi, Pat Mora, or Ana Castillo as Mexican-American; Judith Ortiz Cofer as Puerto Rican; Himilce Novas and Beatriz Rivera as of Cuban origin; or Rima de Vallbona as Costa Rican. However, in other cases, filling in this seemingly simple field was not so clear-cut. First, some authors have mixed heritage, which complicates the assignment of a single category. For instance, Yolanda Gallardo is described as born in the Bronx to parents of Cuban and Venezuelan/Puerto Rican heritage. Information from APP webpage, https://artepublicopress.com/yolanda-gallardo/. Second, the lack of readily accessible information about some writers prevented us from assigning an accurate label.

The issue of explicitly stating origin is closely linked to questions of self-identification and the visibility of ethnic-cultural identity. Terms of identity in this context are particularly complex. The labels Hispanic and Latino/Latina, standardized through U.S. Census and OMB racial and ethnic classifications, function as pan-ethnic categories. While this gives them administrative and statistical utility, it does not resolve the internal differences of nationality, race, class, cultural affiliation, or personal self-identification. The category of Latinidad (especially when “Latino” is conflated with “brown”), often flattens racial distinctions and contributes to the erasure of Afro-Latine and Black Latin American diasporic identities .
Chicano/Chicana frequently carries a political valence, rooted in the Chicano Movement of the 1960s and 1970s; for this reason, many Mexican-Americans choose not to identify with the term. More recent gender-neutral innovations such as Latinx, Latine, Chicanx, and Afro-Latinx have not resolved these debates . Complicating matters further, the category Latino has long been shaped by marketing industries, functioning as an Anglo-hegemonic discursive strategy for selling ethnicity for the U.S. mainstream.

We believed that designations such as Chicana, Latina, or other recent variants within the Hispanic community could only be applied if the author explicitly identified herself as such in the biographical note accompanying the book or on official digital platforms. The terms available for self-designation are the subject of debate. "Chicana" carries a specific political genealogy tied to the Chicano Movement of the 1960s–70s and to Chicana feminist thought. "Latina/o" functions as a broader pan-ethnic term spanning national-origin groups. "Hispanic," the official U.S. Census category, foregrounds a shared linguistic heritage tied to Spain, a framing some critics argue privileges that lineage over Indigenous and Afro-diasporic ones. More recently, gender-neutral alternatives such as "Latinx" and "Latine" have emerged to move beyond Spanish's binary grammatical gender. Given this controversy, we chose to rely on each author's own self-designation rather than impose a single external label.
However, while in some cases this categorization was clear, in others it proved more problematic — either because the author did not identify with these terms or because her self-identification might change over time.

As we progressed in building our database, other issues emerged, particularly in the columns for Genre and Subject. The first refers to terms that correspond to the cataloging treatment of the resource, while the second addresses the thematic categorization of the content. To ensure standardization and interoperability of our system, we decided to adopt terms from the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) cataloging system, given the widespread use of its records. We aimed to use standardized terms to facilitate searches and ensure the interoperability of our information system. As we continued populating our database, we noticed frequent gaps in the LC catalog, which drew our attention.

We discovered that several publications lacked classification in both the Form/Genre and LC Subject Headings fields. For instance, titles such as Women Are Not Roses by Ana Castillo; Woman, Woman (1985), Chants (1984), and Borders (1986) by Pat Mora; Terms of Survival: Poems (1987) by Judith Ortiz Cofer; The Computer Is Down (1987) by Evangelina Vigil-Piñón; and Shadows and Supposes (2002) by Gloria Vando, to name just a few, did not include such classifications. In other cases, the Library of Congress records did not specify a genre. This is evident in works such as The Rebel (1994) by Leonor Villegas de Magnón and its Spanish edition (2004); A Nation of Women (2004) and Absolute Equality (2009) by Luisa Capetillo; African Passions and Other Stories (1995) by Beatriz Rivera; Latina Leadership Lessons (2022) edited by Delia García, among many others.

Conclusively, it is clear that many works within our bibliographic corpus receive a rudimentary or superficial treatment from librarians. This raises questions about how to interpret this lack of attention toward these works. Is it due to a lack of specialized knowledge in Latino Studies among catalogers? Or does it reflect an implicit judgment about the significance of these works? These could be some of the reasons behind the phenomenon of under-cataloging, that is, the omission of records or the provision of too few details. In any case, these omissions highlight the inadequate categorization of literature written by Latina women within conventional library systems, which in turn hinders the visibility of their works and complicates the retrieval of information for researchers and readers interested in exploring this literary corpus.

Nevertheless, since the subject headings system is designed more as an access route to materials within a library than as a summary of a work's content, we have found that it does not help to clarify the actual content of the books included in our bibliographic corpus. To complement this information, we added the "Tags" column, which contains user-generated tags, that is, keywords or informal markers that we deemed relevant to enhance the thematic information of each book. While the use of user tags carries the risk of including subjective terms, we have ensured that these tags are directly related to the content of each book rather than the individual reader’s experience with the work (cf. ). Additionally, we incorporated concepts that are not included in the subject headings, which allows us to provide a more detailed classification for each item.

div.head: 5. Digital tools and Project Management
div.p: The second phase of the project focused on constructing a widely accessible and user-friendly digital portal. To get our website up and running, we needed to create a GitHub repository for our collecting and customize it with our content. There are three versions of CollectionBuilder, and in our case, we chose CollectionBuilder GH, which allows us to create web pages through GitHub Pages. There, we configure the website's design and manage its content. To edit our exhibit, we needed to complete two templates:

list.item: a) Metadata Spreadsheet: A CSV file describing the collection's objects, which we discussed earlier.

b) Folder with the Objects: Images, audio, video links. In our case, this included book covers in JPG format, 16 interviews with the authors in MP3 format, and 3 videos in MP4 format where the authors comment on their books.

div.p: Once all these files were prepared and uploaded to the GitHub repository, we proceeded to configure and visualize the repertory. GitHub itself provides predefined templates for structuring metadata. It is worth noting that the developers of CollectionBuilder have taken great care to produce detailed documentation, including step-by-step tutorials for creating a website. They also provide contact information for direct communication in case of questions and offer user support through various communication channels. During the editing process of our exhibition, we benefited greatly from the valuable guidance of Devin Becker, who responded to our inquiries quickly and efficiently. We would like to take this opportunity to express our gratitude for his support. Below, we present a view of the GitHub repository where our collection is hosted.

figure.figDesc: The repository contains the project files and configuration used to build and maintain the digital collection through CollectionBuilder-GH and GitHub Pages.

div.p: If we access the site from the user view at https://dhcast.github.io/US-Latina/, we can verify that the collection offers various visualization options through a navigation bar that includes eight tabs:

list.item: Home: Provides a general overview and an initial infographic representation of the collection.
Browse: Enables exploration and information retrieval. Users can search and filter content using author names or keywords.
Subject and Location: Displays tag clouds that allow users to examine terms and themes based on frequency of use.

Map: An interactive map generated with Leaflet, facilitating the identification of geolocations associated with the settings of the novels. This feature allows for an exploration of the geospatial distribution of narrative settings.
Timeline: A chronological representation of the collection’s items, enabling historical contextualization of literary production.
Data: A tabular visualization of metadata, offering filtering options and the ability to download data in CSV or Excel formats.
About: An informational page outlining the project’s purpose, target audience, methodology, and the individuals responsible for the resource’s creation.

figure.head: Explore Locations: tag- cloud view for interactive exploration (all locations link to the corresponding works in the collection).
figure.figDesc: The location-based tag cloud enables readers to explore the geographical settings represented in the literary corpus and navigate to associated works.

div.p: These navigation options encourage an active engagement with the collection’s content, enriching the reader’s experience by allowing interactive exploration, contextualizing the retrieved data, and uncovering new information. The collection invites reflection on the history of Latinos in the United States, their values, struggles, traditions, family relationships, and connections to Indigenous heritage and nature. The integration of textual and geospatial data contributes to a deeper understanding of the geocultural landscape of the American Southwest, the historical and linguistic processes shaping the region, and the identification of areas with a high density of references and meanings — or conversely, those with limited representation. Ultimately, the collection serves as a literary radiography of the cultural imagination reflected by Latina authors over the past four decades, encouraging exploration and critical inquiry into this rich legacy. With regard to inclusion and diversity, the bibliographic corpus brings together works by authors of various backgrounds: Mexican, Puerto Rican, Cuban, and Dominican, spanning different generations, beliefs, and social classes. It recovers histories, experiences, and voices of individuals committed to diversity, community-building, and the print culture.

figure.head: View of the Timeline of the collected works.
figure.figDesc: The timeline situates the collected literary works chronologically, enabling readers to explore publication patterns and the historical development of U.S. Latina and Chicana women's literary production.

div.p: The digital collection is designed for a broad and diverse audience, aiming to provide valuable information to both the general public and the academic community. For non-specialized audiences and community members, the platform serves as an accessible reference tool that enhances awareness of Latina women's writing. For researchers, educators, librarians, and students, it aspires to be a key resource for exploring Latina and Chicana literature through the lenses of women's studies, gender studies, and race studies. The platform seeks to facilitate both quantitative and qualitative data visualization and analysis while also fostering new research questions, uncovering potential connections between texts, tracing the (dis)continuity of certain motifs or themes, and encouraging the study of these works using digital methods and tools. Users can leverage the collection as a starting point for future research in U.S. Latinx studies, Chicana feminist history, decolonization, and critical race theory.

One of the project's key strengths is its sustainability, as it provides visitors with various reusable data formats organized into categories such as themes, locations, and chronology. These datasets can be downloaded and repurposed for other research projects. Our aim is to enable their processing with both quantitative and qualitative textual analysis tools such as VoyantTools, Tableau, and MAXQDA. Additionally, the data can be used to generate literary maps that visualize spaces and explore their historical, political, and symbolic significance. Researchers and educators can employ tools like Google My Maps, Topotext, StoryMapJS, Palladio, Carto, GeoNames, ArcGIS, or QGIS to create spatial representations of literary landscapes. Finally, the website is fully optimized for mobile devices, ensuring accessibility and ease of use across different platforms.

div.head: 6.1 The Homogenization of Latinidad in LCSH
div.p: Throughout the construction of this bibliographic corpus, we encountered various challenges that required us to critically reflect on the difficulties we faced. One of the most significant obstacles was the collection of Subject description from the Library of Congress catalog. As previously noted, the absence of information in this field for numerous cataloged works was particularly striking. This omission can be interpreted in several ways, ranging from a lack of time or oversight by catalogers to a potential disregard for these works and their significance within the U.S. print culture. Even when the catalog provided Subject Headings, the descriptions of the works and the authors’ identities were not always satisfactory or adequate. Our work led us to critically examine the semantic descriptors used in the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH), which tend to present a generalized or pan-Latinx perspective of the authors in our study, without delving into more precise categorizations. While our initial intent was to rely on library-supplied subject headings to classify the key themes and interpretative frameworks of recent Latina and Chicana literature authored by women, the limitations of the LCSH system became increasingly evident. It lacks the necessary granularity to fully capture the diversity and complexity of this literary production.

Our experience has shown that the current tags and semantic descriptors do not adequately reflect the differences within the group of Latina authors. Official cataloging systems tend to impose a homogenizing vision of being Latina or Hispanic, failing to capture the complexity of this reality or address social justice demands. Today, Latinidad is conceptualized as a plural, hybrid, and dynamic identity. There is rather a model of multiple Latinities that takes into account the cultural, social, racial, linguistic, economic, political, and generational diversity of Latinas. This diversity manifests itself, among other aspects, in the multiplicity of terms that the authors themselves choose to identify with: Hispano/a, Latino/a, Latin@, Latinx, Latine, Chican@, Chicanx. Some even reject national Latinx labels (Puerto Rican, Chicano, Cuban, Dominican), opting instead for more personal or specific definitions. None of this can be captured by the pre-coordinated term chains of the library-supplied subject headings.

In this context, the best practice would be to respect the designation provided by each author (if they provide one), recognizing that this self-determination can evolve over time. However, the rigid structures of the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) do not allow for this flexibility or capture the richness of the identities that characterize Latina literature in the U.S. This limitation underscores the need to complement traditional cataloging with alternative strategies, such as the use of user-generated tags, for the classification and representation of these works. Our project has sought to address this gap through the “Tags” column, which allows for a more open and contextualized categorization, in dialogue with the identities and experiences of the authors themselves.

div.head: 6.2 What the Word Clouds Reveal
div.p: An examination of the word cloud of Subject visualization reveals these generalizations, as well as the inconsistent and incoherent use of tags related to authors considered Latinas. One of the most striking findings is the high frequency with which the label "Mexican Americans" (authors/women/poetry/families) appears (71 times), compared to "Hispanic Americans" (women, author, neighborhoods) (23) and "Latin America(ns)" (6). This suggests a strong inclination to catalog Latina literary production within the Mexican-American experience, relegating other identities to the background. The LCSH system, like all taxonomies, controls the creation of new subject headings and their synonyms to group similar materials. For "Mexican Americans," the LCSH thesaurus lists two non-preferred terms, "Chicanos" and "Hispanos." The Library of Congress list of "Authorities" includes headings such as "Latino/Chicano history and society" (included in 1999), "Latino communities" (1997), and "Latino voices" (2003), but none of these are applied to our collection. Regarding the term "Latinx," the thesaurus redirects to "Hispanic Americans" and "Latin Americans." On the other hand, the "Chicano" marker (Chicano movement) — surprisingly — only appears once in our collection (Enriqueta Vasquez and The Chicano Movement: Writings from El Grito Del Norte), as it is reserved exclusively to designate the "Chicano movement." When it comes to literary works by Chicanos, the LCSH recommends using sequences such as "American drama/essays/fiction/literature — 'Mexican American authors,'" or "Mexican American drama/essays/fiction/literature" (if the text is in Spanish).

In our collection, relatively few instances distinguish other nationalities through geo-tags — for example, labels such as "Puerto Ricans" appear in 12 books, "Cubans" in 8, and "Costa Ricans" in 2. This structure reinforces the predominance of the “Mexican American” category and diminishes the visibility of other Latino communities, each with its own distinct histories, traditions, and experiences. Furthermore, the assignment of geographic labels is inconsistent: in some cases, such markers are omitted or replaced by generic categories such as “American” or “United States,” lacking the necessary subsequent qualification. This is evident with authors such as Liz DeJesus, María Espinosa, Delilah Montoya, Carol Córdoba, Alicia Gaspar de Alba (in Crimes of the Tongue, The Curse of the Gypsy), and Beatriz Rivera (in Do Not Pass Go), even though in some instances this information is present on the book cover. We recognize that including or excluding certain information in records is inherently a political matter. The omission of specific identity markers and the tendency to homogenize the Latin experience in the United States perpetuate a reductive view of the diversity inherent in Latinx and Chicana literature. This underscores the urgent need to rethink cataloging systems and to adopt approaches that are more inclusive and representative of the multiple Latin identities.

A cursory analysis of the Library of Congress-supplied subject headings further highlights the limitations of the LCSH in accurately reflecting the central themes of Latina writing. When examining the tag cloud generated from the Subject Headings, the lack of representation of specific issues typically associated with this body of literature becomes particularly striking. For instance, although the term border appears explicitly in five titles — Mora’s Borders, Alarcón’s The Border Patrol Ate My Dust, Kabalen & Mijares’ (eds.) Women and Print Culture: A Critical Exploration of the Archives of the Border Region of Mexico and the United States, Sanmiguel’s Under the Bridge: Stories from the Border, and Pérez’s Queering the Border: Essays—only the latter is assigned the subject heading “Mexican-American Border Region”. Moreover, this label appears in only three additional books (Desert Blood: The Juárez Murders; When Mexico Recaptures Texas: Essays; and Intaglio: A Novel in Six Stories), totaling a mere four occurrences in the entire collection. Similarly, the subject heading “immigration” / “immigrants” is associated with only six titles: The Border Patrol Ate My Dust, The Child of Exile: A Poetry Memoir, Litany of Saints: A Triptych, The River Flows North: A Novel, Confessions of a Book Burner: Personal Essays and Stories, and Migrations and Other Stories. These numbers are insufficient to adequately capture the reality of immigration and the border experience represented in this literature, revealing the limitations of current cataloging systems in identifying key themes within this corpus.

Another example of missing terminology is the absence of the subject heading Citizen, which, significantly, does not appear at all. In contrast, the heading “Noncitizens — United States — Biography” is present in only one instance (Córdoba, Stowaways). Similarly, the category Race relations appears in just two titles (Enriqueta Vasquez and the Chicano Movement: Writings from El Grito del Norte and Verdict in the Desert), while “Racism” is mentioned in only one book (Feminism, Nation, and Myth: La Malinche). Likewise, the tags Ethnic relations and Ethnic identity are recorded in only three publications (The Squatter and the Don; Women Warriors of the Afro-Latina Diaspora; and Feminism, Nation, and Myth: La Malinche). Regarding the subject heading “Feminism,” it is used only six times, primarily in reference to 19th-century feminist pioneers such as Luisa Capetillo (two books) and Clotilde Betances Jaeger. It appears just once in connection with the Chicana feminism of the 1960s (Delia’s Song) and in two feminist-focused anthologies: Feminism, Nation, and Myth: La Malinche and Kis sing the Mango Tree: Puerto Rican Women Rewriting American Literature. These findings reveal that the Library of Congress cataloging system fails to accurately capture the thematic depth of Latina literature, thereby limiting its visibility and accessibility within traditional classification frameworks.

div.head: 6.3 Classification, Power, and the Politics of Naming
div.p: Several scholars have highlighted that cataloging systems based on controlled vocabulary, particularly the LCSH reference system, tend to oversimplify, standardize, and impose fixed categories. This inherent rigidity makes them particularly selective, especially in areas such as race and gender. identified significant issues with the Subject Headings assigned to ethnic groups. Regarding the heading Hispanic Americans, he explained that is used to refer also to Latino Americans, Latinos in the United States, Hispanics in the Unites States, Spanish speaking people in the United States, and Spanish surnamed people in the United States . He also questioned the distinction between Hispanic Americans and Latin Americans — United States, stating: The difference is that the Hispanic Americans are United States citizens; the Latin Americans are just here on a visit .

Olson has examined how the LCSH, as a structured language, impacts gender markers and enacts a process of marginalization and exclusion of women and some of our other Othernesses . She further highlights how the taxonomic system subordinates identity categories to others deemed more primary or relevant (e.g., American fiction — women authors). These practices contribute to invisibility and the deprivation of representation. delves deeper into these biases, analyzing the cultural logic of racism embedded in the design of technological systems and the practices of content construction and editing through digital tools.

This pattern of homogenization and omission reflects broader dynamics in how information systems classify and represent communities of color. In Algorithms of Oppression, demonstrates how, in principle neutral information infrastructures — such as search engines, classification schemes, and metadata standards — can encode and reproduce racialized and gendered hierarchies, systematically marginalizing content by and about women of color even in the absence of any single discriminatory actor. In a related vein, concept of transborder knowledge-making highlights how communities historically excluded from dominant archival and bibliographic systems generate their own practices of documentation and representation, often precisely in response to the gaps left by institutions such as the Library of Congress. Read together, these frameworks suggest that the inconsistencies we observe in the LCSH treatment of our own corpus are not isolated cataloging oversights, but a structural feature of information systems that were not designed with Latina and Chicana literary production, or communities of color more broadly.

With these considerations in mind, we recognize lack of terminology to adequately represent ethnic realities within the LC subject heading system — an issue that extends beyond the cataloging of Latinx authors and is similarly present in the classification of other ethnic and racial groups. However, the problem runs deeper, beginning with how data is structured and represented within the Digital Humanities. It is evident that an individual’s perception of their racial and gender identity is far more complex and nuanced than the inherently simplified semantic markers used in controlled vocabularies. We are still in search of a model capable of reflecting these categories with the necessary flexibility, aligning with the lived experiences of individuals in their specific historical and geographical contexts. As Posner argues, a fundamental shift is needed in the very structure of data models for identity. She emphasizes the necessity of ripping apart and rebuilding the machinery of the archive and database so that it does not reproduce the logic that got us here in the first place . Once again, this underscores the fact that merely visualizing datasets generated by cultural institutions is insufficient. Instead, these datasets must be critically reviewed and restructured to prevent the perpetuation of the power dynamics that originally shaped them. As Posner further asserts, the fact that we do not have a really accurate data model of race in this country means that we cannot really understand people’s lived experience of it. Or at least we cannot produce data-driven visualizations that do a very good job of reflecting people’s lived experiences .

div.head: 6.4 Toward More Flexible, Pluralistic Cataloging
div.p: In conclusion, cataloging practices prove insufficient for this body of literature. Once again, it becomes evident that the system does not prioritize the logic of difference, especially with regard to women, queer individuals, and people of color, as emphasized. While this project does not offer a definitive solution to these shortcomings, it underscores the urgent need to rethink more precise strategies for representing the reality of an ethnic culture like Latinx, particularly through a feminist lens. Exploring alternatives is essential. One potential solution could be the incorporation of user-generated tags to complement the subject headings, as suggests. This approach would allow for a more agile adaptation to constantly evolving terminologies and shifting social dynamics. Another possibility would be implementing flexible data models that allow for multiple values in key metadata fields (e.g., having multiple entries for ethnicity or cultural background) to accommodate the complexity of Latinidad. This could involve a more modular metadata schema where new fields or subfields can be added as needed, ensuring that emerging descriptors or self-identifications are captured.

div.head: 7. Conclusion
div.p: In this article, we have outlined the motivations behind our project, as well as the stages of its development and implementation. Our aim was to highlight the Latina women's literature that has been overlooked in U.S. literary history and present it in an open digital space, allowing it to be discovered and valued by a wide audience of readers, educators, and scholars. This work serves as an example of how to create a digital exhibition that collects the narratives, experiences, and knowledge of underrecognized writers, whose work reflects intersectional women’s literary praxis. At the same time, it represents an act of legitimizing the writing of Latinx women, with the purpose of addressing their current underrepresentation and biased portrayal within U.S. culture. Our work contributes to the reimagining of digital humanities practices and cataloging systems in ways that are more inclusive and reflective of the diverse experiences of marginalized communities.

Throughout our research process, we have been pondering the potential of CollectionBuilder not merely to disseminate the works of Latina authors to the general public but also to enhance the possibilities for research and reflection within the academic community on the topics they address. Among its main strengths are undoubtedly its ease of access, an attractive graphic design, the variety of visualization formats, and its full adaptability to mobile devices. However, we also encountered certain technical limitations with this tool. On one hand, it can be noted that the platform in its standard version does not support bilingual editing; on the other hand, its mapping system does not support multiple locations per item. In our case, we were only able to represent a single geographical location per book. This becomes restrictive in novels that address the movement of characters, as such shifts were not reflected in the cartographic visualization. These two issues are solvable but require adaptations in the tool's code — specifically, in the JavaScript for the map and plugins to add multilingual support — modifications that must be requested directly from the developers.
There are ways to set up a multilingual Jekyll site without plugins, but these methods are more technically complex (Simple IT Rocks 2019).
Looking ahead, another interesting challenge would be incorporating features that allow users to add tags or comments, but this would require rethinking the visualizations of the static website.

figure.figDesc: The map displays the geographical locations associated with the literary works, supporting the exploration of spatial patterns in the collection and illustrating the platform's limitation to one mapped location per book.

div.p: By leveraging an open-access site, U.S. Latina Writers makes literary heritage broadly accessible to readers, families, and communities who may not have access to specialized archives. The collection enables Hispanic communities to see their stories, histories, and cultural backgrounds represented, fostering cultural pride and collective memory. Researchers can use the metadata tags to trace motifs across authors and texts, such as migration, border crossings, ancestral storytelling, trauma, and healing. Teachers at both the high school and college levels gain access to an interactive resource that supports new approaches to teaching Latina literature. The timeline and map visualizations help situate Latina authors historically and geographically, while additional visualizations provide entry points for exploring thematic modules (e.g., the evolution of themes by decade, code-switching, hybrid identities, food and culinary memory). The site can serve as a discussion tool in the classroom; for example, students can investigate why certain decades saw more publications, or why certain regions appear underrepresented. To support this use, it may be useful to develop downloadable teacher’s guides or lesson plans aligned with specific modules (e.g., Latina Poetry in the 1990s, Migration experiences in Latina fiction). Community members, libraries, and schools, especially in Latin-majority neighborhoods, can use the portal to explore how their regional histories are reflected in Latina writing. The platform can support reading groups, discussion panels, and “story walks” in which participants share personal connections to the writers featured on the site or narrate their own stories. Its mobile-friendly design further facilitates the use of social media to highlight individual authors, thematic spotlights, or literary anniversaries.

As potential improvements for our collection, we consider it pertinent to augment author-related information and provide a broader cultural and historical framework in the introductory section to properly contextualize the works gathered here. It would also be useful to include additional information regarding the reception of the works, reviews, analytical articles, and other academic works by incorporating links that direct users to secondary bibliographies. Thus, this resource would function not merely as a repository of Latina authorship but also as a platform for critical reflection and continuous scholarly inquiry. Furthermore, having a bilingual version would be desirable to enable collaboration between Spanish and English-speaking communities, thereby expanding the reach and accessibility of the project.

Finally, we recognize that compiling metadata about the texts of female authors published by Arte Público Press is just the first step in providing a valuable online resource about the Latino literary landscape in North America. The works of Chicano/U.S. Latina writers are scattered across various small and medium-sized publishing houses in different parts of the U.S., such as FlowerSong Press, Mouthfeel Press (MFP), and Conocimientos Press, etc. Expanding this collection to include these centers of print culture would allow for a more comprehensive mapping of the literary production of Latina women. This would be a natural and desirable step in the evolution of our tool, as it would significantly contribute to the visibility and recognition of these authors both nationally and internationally.

Taken together, the evidence developed throughout this article converges on a central claim: Library of Congress Subject Headings, structured around fixed, pre-coordinated categories, cannot adequately capture the plural, intersectional, and evolving nature of Latina identity. Our analysis of the collection's own metadata — the overrepresentation of "Mexican Americans" relative to other national-origin categories, and the near-absence of subject headings for border, immigration, and feminist themes central to this literature — demonstrates that this is not a marginal cataloging gap but a structural limitation rooted in how classification systems have historically been built. In response, we have proposed that user-generated tagging and more flexible, pluralistic metadata models, of the kind implemented in our own "Tags" column, offer a partial corrective. They allow for self-determined, evolving identity designations that pre-coordinated subject headings cannot accommodate, without claiming to resolve the deeper structural biases embedded in library classification systems as a whole.

Beyond its immediate contribution to Latina literary bibliography, this project speaks to broader conversations at the intersection of digital humanities, feminist studies, and data science. Within digital humanities, it extends calls to "build otherwise" () and to decolonize digital archival practice (), joining a growing body of scholarship that challenges the presumed neutrality of information systems ; . Within feminist data studies, the project operationalizes the principles of data feminism () at the level of concrete design decisions Their principle of attention to context guided our approach to authorial self-identification. Together with intersectional feminist DH (), this approach models a reflexive practice of metadata and digital curation that other collection-building projects, regardless of subject matter, might adapt. Finally, for the study of U.S. Latino literature, the project builds on Kanellos's account of this literature as a national tradition distinct from Latin American letters, and on Caminero-Santangelo's understanding of latinidad as a constructed category, translating those insights into a working bibliographic infrastructure, one that treats the instability and plurality of Latina identity as a feature of the literature itself that metadata practices must learn to hold.
